content: Depression is a common mood disorder characterized by a persistently low mood, reduced interest in activities, and a loss of pleasure. Music therapy has been proposed as a potential intervention to regulate mood and emotions in individuals with depression. An updated review of the 2008 Cochrane analysis was conducted to better understand the effects of music therapy on depression. The primary objectives of this review were twofold: first, to evaluate the effects of music therapy on depression in individuals of any age compared to treatment as usual (TAU), psychological therapies, pharmacological therapies, or other interventions; and second, to compare the effects of different types of music therapy in individuals diagnosed with depression. To achieve these objectives, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, Web of Science, PsycInfo, CINAHL, Embase, PubMed, and others. The search covered studies up to September 2016, with an update in August 2017. Reference lists of relevant articles and systematic reviews were also examined, and trialists and experts were contacted for additional information. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials (CCTs) comparing music therapy to other interventions were included. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were calculated for continuous data, and odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for dichotomous data, both with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. The review included nine studies with a total of 421 participants, of whom 411 were included in the meta-analysis examining the short-term effects of music therapy on depression. Moderate-quality evidence demonstrated that music therapy combined with TAU had a significant positive effect on depressive symptoms compared to TAU alone. This was observed for both clinician-rated depressive symptoms (SMD -0.98, 95% CI -1.69 to -0.27, based on three RCTs and one CCT, n = 219) and patient-reported depressive symptoms (SMD -0.85, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.34, based on three RCTs and one CCT, n = 142). Importantly, music therapy was not associated with an increased or decreased risk of adverse events compared to TAU. Regarding secondary outcomes, music therapy combined with TAU was more effective than TAU alone in reducing anxiety and improving functioning. However, it did not show a significant advantage in improving quality of life (SMD 0.32, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.80, P = 0.20, n = 67, low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in the number of participants who discontinued the study early (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.70, P = 0.26, based on five RCTs and one CCT, n = 293, moderate-quality evidence). The meta-analysis suggests that music therapy, when added to TAU, provides short-term benefits for individuals with depression compared to TAU alone. However, the evidence regarding the comparison of music therapy to psychological therapies is uncertain. For clinician-rated depressive symptoms, the evidence was of very low quality (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -2.36 to 0.81, based on one RCT, n = 11). Similarly, for patient-reported depressive symptoms, the evidence was of low quality (SMD -1.28, 95% CI -3.75 to 1.02, based on four RCTs, n = 131). The effects on quality of life (SMD -1.31, 95% CI -0.36 to 2.99, based on one RCT, n = 11) and study discontinuation rates (OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.49, based on four RCTs, n = 157) were also uncertain. No eligible evidence was found to address the effects of music therapy on adverse events, functioning, or anxiety when compared to psychological therapies. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether one form of music therapy is superior to another. For clinician-rated depressive symptoms, patient-reported depressive symptoms, quality of life, and study discontinuation rates, the evidence was of very low quality, and no eligible data were available for adverse events, functioning, or anxiety. In conclusion, the findings of this meta-analysis indicate that music therapy provides short-term benefits for individuals with depression, particularly when combined with TAU. It appears to improve depressive symptoms, reduce anxiety, and enhance functioning without increasing the risk of adverse events. However, further research with robust study designs and larger sample sizes, particularly in children and adolescents, is needed to confirm these findings. Future studies should also investigate the mechanisms underlying the effects of music therapy and provide detailed descriptions of the interventions and comparators to ensure reproducibility and facilitate comparisons.
